setup: Freecone pays 3.0% fixed and receives six-month SOFR on USD 50.0m, semi-annually, with 1.25 years left (payments in 0.25, 0.75 and 1.25 years). The next floating rate was set at 2.40%. The SOFR curve is flat at 2.60% continuously compounded, and SOFR is also the discount rate.
ask: Freecone's current exposure on the swap (the positive part of its mark-to-market) is:

options.label: Zero: the mark-to-market is negative, so exposure floors at 0
About +USD 0.34m: the swap is an asset to Freecone
options.why: Flipped the sign of the mark-to-market. Freecone receives floating (2.4%, then about 2.6%) and pays 3.0%, so every net payment is a small outflow.

options.label: About USD 0.34m: the size of the mark-to-market, whatever its sign
options.why: Used the absolute value. Exposure is $\max(V, 0)$: a negative mark-to-market is what the bank owes, not what it stands to lose.

takeaway: Paying 3.0% against floating rates of 2.4% to 2.6% means the swap is out of the money, so current exposure is zero however large the negative value.

setup: A portfolio's future value is normally distributed with mean USD 0 and standard deviation USD 10m. The 95% one-sided normal quantile is 1.645.
ask: 95% potential future exposure (PFE) is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 1.6m
options.why: Left out $\sigma$: used the 1.645 z-score as if it were already in dollars.

options.label: ≈ USD 4.0m
options.why: Gave the expected exposure $\sigma\phi(0) = 0.399 \times 10$ instead of the 95th percentile.

options.label: ≈ USD 165m
options.why: Multiplied the z-score by the variance (100) instead of the standard deviation.

takeaway: PFE is a high percentile of the future value (about 1.6 standard deviations here); expected exposure is only about 0.4 standard deviations.

setup: A one-year trade has expected exposure (USD m) of 0.20, 0.35, 0.30, 0.40 and 0.25 at t = 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1.0 years. Effective EE is the non-decreasing version of EE: at each date it is the larger of that date's EE and the previous effective EE.
ask: Effective EE at t = 1.0 year is:

options.label: USD 0.25m
options.why: Read off the raw EE at t = 1.0. Effective EE never falls below an earlier value, and EE already reached 0.40 at t = 0.8.

options.label: USD 0.34m
options.why: Averaged the effective EE path (that is the effective EPE, one number for the whole profile), not the value at one date.

options.label: USD 0.35m
options.why: Stopped the running maximum at the 0.4-year peak and missed the new high of 0.40 at t = 0.8.

takeaway: Effective EE is a running maximum: once exposure has peaked, the effective figure holds that level for the rest of the profile.

setup: For a zero-mean normal mark-to-market, expected exposure is approximately $EE(t) \approx 0.4\,\sigma\sqrt{t}$. The exposure has volatility $\sigma = 9.0\%$ per annum, with 250 trading days per year.
ask: Expected exposure after 10 trading days is closest to:

options.why: Used $t = 0.04$ without the square root: $0.4 \times 9.0\% \times 0.04$.
Left out the time factor altogether: $0.4 \times 9.0\%$ is the one-year figure.
Put 10 (days) in as if it were years: $\sqrt{10} = 3.16$ instead of $\sqrt{0.04} = 0.2$.

takeaway: Exposure grows with the square root of time, and the clock must be in years: 10 days is a fifth of a one-year EE, not 4% of it.

setup: A derivative's future value (USD m) is +10, +6, +3, +1, −1, −3, −6 or −10 with probabilities 5%, 10%, 15%, 20%, 20%, 15%, 10% and 5%. The distribution is symmetric, so its mean is zero.
ask: The expected exposure (EE) of the position is:

options.label: Positive: only the gains count, so the average cannot be zero
Zero: gains and losses cancel in a symmetric distribution
options.why: Averaged the future value instead of the exposure. The expected value is zero, but exposure is $\max(V, 0)$, and the losses are floored at 0 rather than netted.

takeaway: Expected exposure is the mean of the positive part, so it is positive whenever any outcome is positive, even when the expected value is zero.

setup: An exposure profile has EE (USD m) of 3, 5, 8, 6 and 2, each held constant over the interval ending at dates 0.5, 1, 2, 3 and 5 years (interval lengths 0.5, 0.5, 1, 1 and 2 years). The plain average of the five EE figures is 4.8.
ask: The time-weighted EPE over the five years is:

options.label: Above 4.8
options.why: Assumed the peak of 8 pulls the average up. But the low EE of 2 sits in the longest interval (2 years), while the 3 and 5 last only half a year each.

options.label: Equal to 4.8
options.why: Used the plain average of the five numbers, which treats a 6-month interval and a 2-year interval as equal weights.

takeaway: EPE averages over time, not over observation dates: the longer an exposure level lasts, the more it counts.

setup: At one future date a netting set has five equally likely mark-to-market outcomes to the bank (USD m): +40, +20, 0, −20, −30.
ask: Expected exposure (EE) at that date is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 2m
options.why: Averaged the raw outcomes, losses included: that is the expected mark-to-market, $(40 + 20 + 0 - 20 - 30)/5$.

options.label: ≈ USD 30m
options.why: Averaged only the positive outcomes, $(40 + 20)/2$. The three scenarios with zero exposure still carry weight in the average.

options.label: ≈ USD 110m
options.why: Added up the sizes of all five outcomes, positive and negative, and never divided by 5.

takeaway: EE is the probability-weighted average of the positive part over all outcomes: losses count as zero exposure but keep their probability weight.

setup: A CLO waterfall is run on 1,000 simulated default threads. For the mezzanine bond the mean loss is USD 0.62m, the 10th-highest loss is USD 3.40m and the 50th-highest is USD 1.90m. Credit VaR is measured as the loss quantile minus the expected loss.
ask: The 99% credit VaR, compared with USD 3.40m, is:

options.label: Below USD 3.40m: the expected loss comes off the quantile
Equal to USD 3.40m: the quantile is the VaR
options.why: Reported the 99% loss quantile (10th of 1,000 is the top 1%) without netting off the 0.62 expected loss, as this definition requires.

options.label: Above USD 3.40m: the expected loss is added on
options.why: Added the expected loss instead of subtracting it. VaR here is the unexpected part of the loss.

takeaway: Credit VaR on this definition is the quantile loss less the expected loss, so it sits below the raw tail loss.

setup: A CVA analyst has counterparty credit spreads of 90, 110 and 130bp at 1, 2 and 3 years, with 40% recovery. The average hazard rate to maturity $T$ is spread/(1 − R) and survival is $e^{-\bar\lambda T}$. The 3-year average hazard is $\bar\lambda(3) = 2.17\%$ and $V(2) = 0.964$. The probability of default in year 3 is $q_3 = V(2) - V(3)$.
ask: $q_3$ compared with the 3-year average hazard of 2.17% is:

options.label: Below 2.17%
options.why: Took the 2.17% average and shrank it for survival to year 2 (2.17% × 0.964 ≈ 2.09%). But the year-3 hazard is not the average: on a rising curve it is about 2.83%.

options.label: Equal to 2.17%
options.why: Used the average hazard to year 3 as if it were the default rate inside year 3. With spreads still widening, year 3's own hazard is higher.

takeaway: A rising spread curve means the forward hazard in a later year (here about 2.8%) is above the average hazard to that date; the interval default probability follows the forward rate.

setup: An issuer has one zero-coupon bond: face JPY 50.0bn, 4 years to maturity. A calibrated Merton model gives firm assets of JPY 68.0bn and equity of JPY 24.5bn. The risk-free rate is 1.5% continuously compounded. The credit spread is the debt's continuously compounded yield $y$ (from $D = Fe^{-yT}$) minus the risk-free rate.
ask: The credit spread on the debt is closest to:

options.label: ≈ 20 bps
options.why: Scale slip (1/10): treated 1.98% as 0.198%.

options.label: ≈ 498 bps
options.why: Added the risk-free rate to the 3.48% yield instead of subtracting it.

options.label: ≈ 1,243 bps
options.why: Forgot to divide the log by $T = 4$: $0.1393 - 0.015$ gives 12.4%.

takeaway: Debt = assets minus equity; the spread is the extra yield over risk-free, and the log of the debt-to-face ratio must be annualised by $T$.

setup: Two one-year zero-coupon bonds of the same issuer, with the same default probability and risk-neutral pricing. Risk-free rate 3.0%. The senior bond yields 5.5% with a 45% recovery rate; the subordinated bond recovers only 15%.
ask: The subordinated bond's yield spread over the risk-free rate is closest to:

options.label: 2.5%, the same as the senior bond
options.why: Same default probability does not mean same spread. The spread prices expected loss, PD × LGD, and the subordinated bond's LGD is higher.
Scaled the senior 2.5% by 85/45. The senior LGD is 1 − 45% = 55%, so the ratio is 85/55 = 1.55.
Scaled by the ratio of recovery rates (45/15 = 3). Spreads follow loss given default (55% vs 85%), not recovery.

takeaway: With one default probability, spreads scale with LGD: here 85/55 ≈ 1.55 times the senior spread.

setup: One-factor Gaussian copula for a granular loan book: average one-year PD 1.5%, correlation $\rho = 0.12$, 99.9% confidence. Worst-case default rate $= N\!\left(\frac{N^{-1}(PD) + \sqrt{\rho}\,N^{-1}(0.999)}{\sqrt{1-\rho}}\right)$, with $N^{-1}(0.015) = -2.170$ and $N^{-1}(0.999) = 3.090$.
ask: The 99.9% worst-case default rate is about how many times the 1.5% average?

options.label: About 1×: the same as the average
options.why: Dropped the correlation term. With $\rho = 0$ the argument is just $N^{-1}(PD)$ and the worst case equals the average PD.

options.label: About 2×
options.why: Used $\rho = 0.12$ in place of $\sqrt{\rho} = 0.346$, so the stress term was far too small: the argument is −1.92, giving about 2.8%.

takeaway: Correlation makes the 1-in-1,000 default rate a multiple of the average, here about 8 times. Note the factor loading is $\sqrt{\rho}$, not $\rho$.

setup: Firm A has assets of USD 1,000m funded by USD 600m of debt at 4% and USD 400m of equity. EBIT is USD 90m before credit losses of USD 50m. Tax is 25% of positive pre-tax income.
ask: Firm A's ROE after credit losses is closest to:

options.why: Ignored the credit losses: $(90 - 24) \times 0.75 / 400$.
Forgot the interest on the debt: $(90 - 50) \times 0.75 / 400$.
Skipped the tax: pre-tax income of 16 over equity of 400.

takeaway: Leverage amplifies ROE only if the asset return exceeds the cost of debt; credit losses and tax come off before dividing by equity.

setup: A revolving facility has a USD 5.0m limit, of which USD 2.5m is drawn today. For the next 12 months the analyst sets PD at 2%, expects the drawn balance at default to be USD 3.2m, and expects to recover 55% of a defaulted balance.
ask: Which amount belongs in $EL = PD \times EAD \times LGD$ as EAD?

options.label: USD 3.2m, the balance expected at default
USD 2.5m, today's drawn balance
options.why: Used the current balance. Borrowers tend to draw more as they approach default, so EAD is the expected drawn amount at default; this would give EL = USD 22,500.

options.label: USD 5.0m, the full limit
options.why: Assumed the line is fully drawn at default. That ignores the analyst's estimate of USD 3.2m and would overstate EL at USD 45,000.

takeaway: EAD is the exposure expected at default, not today's drawn amount and not the limit.

reading: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
setup: A mortgage score band has a historical annual loss rate of 2.4%, where loss rate = PD × LGD, and an LGD of 60%.
ask: The implied PD of the band is:

options.label: Below 2.4% (about 1.4%)
options.why: Multiplied the loss rate by LGD: $2.4\% \times 0.6 = 1.44\%$. That is applying LGD twice, since the loss rate already includes it.

options.label: Equal to 2.4%
options.why: Treated the loss rate as if it were the default rate, which holds only if LGD were 100%.

takeaway: Loss rate is PD scaled down by LGD, so going back to PD must scale up: any LGD below 100% puts PD above the loss rate.

setup: One-year transitions: a B-rated credit goes to A with 10%, stays B with 70% and defaults with 20%; an A-rated credit stays A with 80% and falls to B with 20% (A cannot default directly); default is absorbing. Years are independent. A USD 15.0m loan to a B-rated borrower runs for three years.
ask: The three-year cumulative probability of default for the B-rated borrower is closest to:

options.why: Used the one-year default probability and ignored that the borrower can default in year 2 or 3.
Added three years of 20%. Only the borrowers who have not yet defaulted can default later, and some of the 20% each year is already gone.

takeaway: Cumulative PD sums default paths over the years, each weighted by survival; it is well below the sum of the annual rates. EL on the loan is $15.0 \times 44.2\% \times 60\% = $ USD 3.98m.

setup: A BBB-rated company has a 91.93% chance of keeping its rating over one year, and rating changes in different years are independent. Taking off 8.07 points for each of four years would give 67.7%.
ask: The true four-year probability of still being BBB is:

options.label: Below 67.7%
options.why: Thought risks pile up faster than a straight line. But each year's 8.07% loss applies only to the shrinking share still BBB, so the later losses are smaller than 8.07 points.

takeaway: Independent annual retention compounds multiplicatively: $p^n$, which stays above the straight-line $1 - n(1-p)$.

setup: In a default-correlation framework each of eight firms either defaults or survives over the horizon. A joint outcome says which of the eight firms defaulted.
ask: The number of distinct joint default/survival outcomes is closest to:

options.why: Added instead of multiplied: $2 \times 8$.
Squared the number of firms: $8^2$.
Counted orderings of the firms, $8! = 40{,}320$, rather than default/survive states.

takeaway: Binary outcomes multiply: $n$ firms give $2^n$ joint outcomes, which is why default-correlation frameworks explode in size.

setup: In a single-factor model each firm's asset return is $a_i = \beta_i m + \sqrt{1-\beta_i^2}\,\epsilon_i$, with $m$ and every $\epsilon_i$ independent standard normals. Firm X has $\beta = 0.8$ and Firm Y has $\beta = 0.9$.
ask: The correlation between the asset returns of X and Y is:

options.label: Between 0.80 and 0.90
options.why: Averaged the two betas (0.85). The only link between the firms is the common factor, so the correlation is the product, not a mean.

options.label: Above 0.90
options.why: Added the betas (1.7) or took the larger one. A correlation cannot exceed 1, and betas below 1 multiply to something smaller than either.

takeaway: In the single-factor model, correlation is the product of the two betas, so it is below both of them.

setup: In the single-factor model two firms in the same industry share the same beta to the market factor, and the correlation between their asset returns is estimated at 0.36.
ask: The beta of each firm is closest to:

options.why: Squared the correlation instead of taking its root.
Split the correlation between the two firms, $0.36/2$. Betas multiply, they do not add.
Set beta equal to the correlation. That would give $\rho = 0.36^2 = 0.13$.

takeaway: With equal betas, asset correlation is $\beta^2$, so each beta is the square root of the correlation, and larger than it.

setup: A copula simulation of two USD 1.0m loans gives 1,000 one-year scenarios. Portfolio loss is USD 1.0m in 8 scenarios, USD 0.6m in 22, USD 0.4m in 40 and zero in the other 930.
ask: Counting from the worst scenario, the loss of the 10th-worst scenario (the 99% level) is:

options.label: USD 1.0m
options.why: Took the maximum loss. Only the 8 worst scenarios (0.8%) lose 1.0m; the 10th worst is already past them.

options.label: USD 0.4m
options.why: Went too far into the tail: the 10th worst is within the 22 scenarios at 0.6m (ranks 9 to 30). Losses of 0.4m start at rank 31.

working.label: Ranks by loss
working.display: ranks 1–8 lose 1.0m; ranks 9–30 lose 0.6m; ranks 31–70 lose 0.4m

working.label: 99% credit VaR
working.display: rank 10 is in the 0.6m group $\Rightarrow$ USD 0.6m

takeaway: Quantile from a simulation: rank the losses from the worst and read the entry at the tail-probability mark.
